title: Enhancing Quality and Security in CI: Gunjan Patel
talk_summary: Gunjan Patel describes a 'ghost pilot' CI pipeline that deliberately (not in real-time) improves variable names/comments, then generates unit tests in staged passes (baseline behavior, adversarial edge cases, historical-bug personalization), then runs a multi-agent red-team/developer/manager debate to find and prioritize security issues, proposing fixes for human review. The core mechanism is slow, iterative, context-rich LLM passes in CI rather than one-shot 'generate tests/find bugs' prompts.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of one prompt 'generate unit tests', they first have the LLM state expected behavior from comments/README/PRD, then a separate adversarial pass lists edge cases (boundary, min/max, weird chars) without writing tests, then personalize with team priorities and historical bugs, then generate tests and loop until they pass.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's not asking an llm to say generate unit test for this code it doesn't do a very good job ... this is where having iterations comes into play

takeaways.technique: Pre-review normalization pass (rename vars, fix comments)
takeaways.what_they_do: First CI step has the LLM improve variable names and code comments to make intent explicit before any test generation or review, so downstream LLM passes have clearer semantics.
takeaways.evidence_quote: improving code comments ... to make sure that llms understand what is intended behavior of this code even though even if the code may not reflected

takeaways.technique: Role-debate for security triage with self-reflection
takeaways.what_they_do: Simulates three AI employees (red-team engineer with security policies, python dev as code author with PRD, engineering manager with business context from transcripts/Slack) that take turns debating each security issue's risk and fix effort, then a separate model self-reflects on whether the conclusion matches original intent.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is a prompt to have these three people take turn multi-turn and then debate among each other on each of the security issues

takeaways.what_they_do: A context file captures cloud provider, service, deployment target, internal vs customer-facing, PII presence, front/back-end, networking, PRD link, bug-tracker project, Slack channel, and infosec policies; the LLM infers language/type and focus areas from historical bugs and escalations.
takeaways.evidence_quote: personalizing happens from Team priority that are written in context. yaml file

takeaways.what_they_do: Uses LLM to find security best-practice violations and logical-flow bugs (e.g., a misplaced safe-statement in a Kubernetes controller) that static analysis misses, then prioritizes which to fix rather than dumping all findings.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this wouldn't have been picked up in any of the SAS tools because it's a logical thing

takeaways.technique: Human-in-the-loop fix proposals with reasoning + policy citation
takeaways.what_they_do: For each proposed fix, the pipeline explains why it's prioritized, summarizes the multi-agent debate into three bullets, cites the security policy, and runs unit tests before a human sees it, so the reviewer only decides which fixes to accept.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for each of the fix explain the reasoning why it's prioritized ... summarized in three bullet points ... so human reviewer has the context
